newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary sees repo cut, O/N rate rise shakes market.
newsitem.headline: Hungary sees repo cut, O/N rate rise shakes market.

text.p: Hungarian overnight interbank interest rates surprised the market on Wednesday with a 1.5 percentage point rise, triggered by repo rate cut expectations, dealers said.
"The forint market was in a swarm," said Sandor Tolonics of Commerzbank. "Repo rate cuts are believed to be timely, and we already felt yesterday that a very sensitive money shortage appeared."
Overnight rates opened at Tuesday's closing levels, 21.50 percent and climbed up to 23.00 percent as only a few market players wanted to lend money, dealers said.
Overnight rates usually hover around the one-week reverse repo rate, which is currently 21 percent.
Dealers said the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) has recently reduced its repo rates with an almost monthly regularity, in line with declining inflation.
A new cut, probably of 0.25 percentage points, was likely to come soon, dealers said.
To take advantage of the current higher reverse repo days, the commercial banks lent to the NBH for one week or one month, drying up most of the market's liquidity, dealers said.
"I bet that everybody placed even the last coin in reverse repo," Tolonics said. "Only those lent in the market who have to manage daily liquidity."
The central bank last cut four of its five repo facilites on February 17, by 0.5 percentage point each. The NBH usually reduces its repo rates on Mondays.

Despite the strengthening repo cut expectations, the sharp rise of overnight rates caught many dealers unguarded as the market's liquidity had been seen being boosted by government bond maturities and interest payments this week.
Some dealers estimated the extra funds from the government payments would total some 80 billion forints this week.
Dealers said substantial funds would enter the market on Thursday, when the government pays interest on the bonds issued in the framework of the bank consolidation programme.
However, personal income tax, VAT and other tax payments, due on Thursday, would have a tightening impact on market liquidity.
